approachQuestion.prompt:
Labeling a Code

A device accepts labels only when they are formed by joining words from a supplied dictionary. Given a non-empty string `code` and a set `words`, return every valid segmentation as a list of words in original order. A word may be reused. Return each segmentation once, in any order.

Constraints: 1 <= code.length <= 24; `code` and every word contain lowercase English letters; 1 <= words.length <= 30; words are distinct and non-empty; each word has length at most 6. The result may contain exponentially many segmentations. The dictionary is supplied as a set with expected O(1) membership checks; the input is not modified.

Example 1: code="sunrise", words={"sun","rise","sunr","ise"} -> [["sun","rise"],["sunr","ise"]].
Example 2: code="mint", words={"mi","nt","mint"} -> [["mint"],["mi","nt"]].
Example 3: code="abx", words={"a","b","ab"} -> [] (the unmatched final character leaves no complete segmentation).

options.text: At each starting position, try each ending position up to six characters later. If that substring is in the dictionary, append it, recurse from the next position, then remove it; emit a copy only upon reaching the end of the code.
options.feedback: Every segmentation has a first word ending at one of these tried boundaries. Advancing the start after a match makes progress, while undo restores the path before the next boundary is explored.

options.text: At each position, choose the longest dictionary word that matches there, then continue after that word.
options.feedback: The longest local match can prevent a complete segmentation. For code="abcd" and words={"abc","ab","cd"}, choosing "abc" leaves "d", while ["ab","cd"] is valid.

options.text: Generate every way to split the code between adjacent characters, then check whether all pieces are dictionary words.
options.feedback: This is correct but does not use dictionary membership to reject a partial split as soon as its next piece is invalid.

options.text: Try boundaries from left to right, but when a piece is absent from the dictionary, keep it in the path and continue from its end.
options.feedback: This can emit invalid labels. For code="ab" and words={"a"}, it may accept ["a","b"] even though "b" is not an allowed word.

feedback.reason: Choose a method that tries valid next boundaries from the current position, emits only complete segmentations, and keeps the current path safe while exploring alternatives.
details: Start at position zero with an empty path. Try every ending position from one through six characters later, stopping at the end of the code. For each dictionary word found, append it, continue from its ending position, and remove it on return. When the position reaches the code length, append a copy of the current path to the results. Each result has one unique sequence of word boundaries; copying the path prevents later undo operations from changing a result already emitted.

A cut position identifies the next suffix to label. Try only dictionary-approved pieces, and accept only at full code exhaustion. Copy completed paths; retaining a shared path reference would make later undo erase earlier segmentations.

If that substring is in the dictionary, append it, recurse from the next position, then remove it; emit a copy only upon reaching the end of the code.”: Every segmentation has a first word ending at one of these tried boundaries. Advancing the start after a match makes progress, while undo restores the path before the next boundary is explored.

“At each position, choose the longest dictionary word that matches there, then continue after that word.”: The longest local match can prevent a complete segmentation. For code="abcd" and words={"abc","ab","cd"}, choosing "abc" leaves "d", while ["ab","cd"] is valid.

“Generate every way to split the code between adjacent characters, then check whether all pieces are dictionary words.”: This is correct but does not use dictionary membership to reject a partial split as soon as its next piece is invalid.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For `boundary-recursion-with-undo`, let n be the code length, V the actual number of recursive states visited including the root and terminal states, and R the total number of characters copied into all returned segmentations. Choose the expected running-time and worst-case auxiliary-space pair. There are at most six candidate words at each state; candidate substrings have length at most six and dictionary membership has expected constant cost. Exclude the supplied code, dictionary, and returned segmentations; include recursion, current path, and output-copying work.

options.text: Expected O(V + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space
Expected O(n² + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space
Expected O(V + R) time, O(V + R) auxiliary space
Worst-case O(V·D + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space, where D is the number of dictionary words

feedback.reason: Bounded-length word trials give constant expected work per visited state plus output copying.
details: There are at most six bounded-length candidates per visited state, so expected dictionary and substring work is constant per state. Visiting V states costs expected O(V); copying complete segmentations adds R. The recursion stack and current path use O(n) auxiliary space.

Each recursive state checks at most six candidate words. Candidate slicing and hashing are constant work because word length is bounded by six; dictionary lookup is expected O(1) by the stated model. Thus search work is expected O(V), and copying all emitted words adds Θ(R). V is the actual state count and may itself be exponential in n; the bound does not claim V is at most 2ⁿ.

Every recursive transition consumes at least one character, so call depth and the current path are at most n. The returned copies belong to output and are excluded; no collection of previously computed suffix answers is kept.

Expected running time under expected O(1) dictionary membership and worst-case auxiliary space. At most six candidate words of length at most six are checked per state. Stack and current path count as auxiliary space; supplied input and returned segmentations do not.
“Expected O(n² + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The number of visited states V can grow exponentially with n, so n² does not bound the search work.
“Expected O(V + R) time, O(V + R) auxiliary space”: This counts returned output or an unneeded table of states as auxiliary space; the method retains only its active recursion path.

“Worst-case O(V·D + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space, where D is the number of dictionary words”: This assumes worst-case dictionary lookup, while the problem explicitly supplies an expected O(1) membership model. Under the stated model, expected O(V+R) is the matching bound.
